Attacker-controlled source: request.getCookies() -> theCookie.getValue() where cookie name equals 'BenchmarkTest00001', URLDecoder.decode(...,"UTF-8") into param. Flow: param concatenated at fileName = Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + param with no validation/canonicalization, then sink at line 72: new java.io.File(fileName) -> new java.io.FileInputStream(...). Only encoder on path is ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML() applied to response output, not to fileName before open, and is inadequate for path traversal (does not strip '../', '/', '\').
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Raw cookie value is URL-decoded and directly concatenated to base directory and passed to FileInputStream with no allowlist, canonical-path check, or FilenameUtils.getName sanitization, allowing '../' traversal outside TESTFILES_DIR.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Authenticated/unauthenticated remote attacker can set cookie to traverse directories (e.g., '../../etc/passwd') and the servlet reads first 1000 bytes and reflects contents in response, yielding arbitrary local file disclosure.
remediation: Canonicalize and validate: resolve File(TESTFILES_DIR, param).getCanonicalPath() and verify it starts with canonical base directory, reject otherwise.
Apply allowlist / strip path components (e.g., FilenameUtils.getName) and reject values containing '/', '\', '..' or null bytes

No HTTP/request/user input flows to this value in shown code. Source is trusted server-side config file, not attacker-controlled, with hard-coded package prefix constraining class name.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/ThingFactory.root_cause: Not externally-controlled input: class name comes from trusted bundled properties file (thing.properties), not user input. Hard-coded prefix 'org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.' plus cast to ThingInterface further restricts instantiation. CWE-470 requires attacker ability to select class/method, which is absent here.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/ThingFactory.impact: If truly attacker-controlled, Class.forName/newInstance would allow unintended instantiation and control-flow bypass. Not exploitable here as attacker cannot control thing.properties without prior host compromise.
remediation: No code change required for this finding - trusted config source.
For defense-in-depth, validate property against explicit allow-list (e.g., Thing1/Thing2) before Class.forName if config file writability is a concern.

org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/Utils.java:1.exploitability_evidence: Flagged sink is Files.setPosixFilePermissions(script.toPath(), perms) at lines 149-157. Source values are hardcoded constants: OWNER_READ/WRITE/EXECUTE + GROUP_READ/EXECUTE + OTHERS_READ/EXECUTE = 0755 (rwxr-xr-x). Target File comes from getFileFromClasspath("insecureCmd.sh") - trusted classpath resource, not attacker-controlled. No attacker-controlled source flows to permission set. The rule claims read+write+exec for all users (0777), but code grants WRITE only to OWNER, which is standard least-privilege for an executable script needing execute bit restored after WAR explosion.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/Utils.java:1.root_cause: Rule misfired: hardcoded 0755 permissions are not overly permissive. World/group write bits are not set. 0755 is the minimal conventional mode for an executable shell script (owner rwx, others r-x). Scanner incorrectly generalized any READ+WRITE+EXECUTE presence as world-writable.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/Utils.java:1.impact: No security impact if unaddressed. If this were true 0777 (world-writable + executable), impact would be tampering/privilege escalation, but that condition does not exist here.
remediation: No fix required - 0755 is appropriate for executable script
If strict least-privilege desired, reduce to OWNER-only (0700/0500) and verify app server user can still execute insecureCmd.sh

remediation: Retain ESAPI_Encoder.encodeForLDAP() on all user input placed in LDAP filters
Do not remove or bypass encoding; add regression test verifying special chars like *()\ are escaped

org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/DatabaseHelp.impact: If caller passes attacker-controlled input, SQL injection could allow data disclosure, modification, authentication bypass, or database command execution.
